title: Kathina
hookLine: at the end of the rains lay people offer cloth for new robes

cards: Thirty monks set out to see the Buddha. Forest monks from a town called Pava, planning to spend the rainy season near him at Savatthi.
But the start of the rains catches them on the road, six yojanas short, as the text counts it. The rule is the rule: stay in one place.

So they spend three whole months stuck at Saketa, close enough to picture him, too far to reach. When the retreat ends, they set off through rain and deep mud, and arrive soaked, robes filthy and heavy with water.
What happens next, tradition says, is the root of a festival Theravada monasteries still keep after the rains.

teach.h: A NEW ALLOWANCE: CLOTH FOR ROBES.
teach.b: The story is in the Vinaya, the monastic rulebook. The Buddha welcomes the thirty, asks how their retreat went, and hears about the waiting and the mud.
He answers with a new allowance: at the end of the rains, monks who have kept the retreat may receive cloth and make new robes. That is the kathina.
The word means firm, or hard, and tradition explains it as the wooden frame the cloth was stretched on for sewing.
In the old practice, the whole community worked together, cutting, sewing and dyeing, to finish a robe in a single day. What makes it a festival?

teach.h: MONKS CAN'T ASK; IT MUST BE OFFERED.
teach.b: Monks aren't allowed to ask for cloth. It has to be offered. So lay people do the offering.

Within a month after the rains end, in Thailand, Laos, Myanmar, Sri Lanka and Cambodia, families and villages organize kathina ceremonies: processions, music, food, money trees hung with small gifts for the monastery, and at the center, a bolt of cloth.
The cloth goes to the community as a whole, not to one favorite monk. The monks agree together which of them will receive it, traditionally one whose robes are most worn.
The rains began with staying still; they end with giving. Three months of practice in one place, then a day of thank you, with something useful.
Not money for its own sake, not a trophy: cloth, for the robe a monk wears every day.

how: In Theravada countries, within a month after the rains retreat ends, lay people hold kathina ceremonies with processions and food, offering robe cloth and other necessities to the monastic community.

o: cloth offered to monks for new robes after the rains
a monk's vow to wear one robe until it wears out
the spring new year, celebrated by splashing water

games.q: you're one of the thirty monks. the rains begin while you're still six yojanas from the Buddha. what do you do?
o: keep walking; seeing him matters more.
stop and keep the retreat where you are.
games.why: they kept the rule and spent the rains at Saketa, then went to him soaked the moment it ended. the Buddha answered with the kathina.

practice: Bring to mind someone who has been steady for you lately, a colleague, a neighbor, a teacher, someone at home, and think about what they'd actually use: a meal, a tool, a warm pair of socks, an hour of help, a book they mentioned.
Let one gift come to mind, and notice the gladness of planning it, the first of the three gladnesses you met in the giving week. Then rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Kathina. The robe-cloth offering at the end of the rains, named for the firm frame the cloth was stretched on.

orig.note: Pali: firm or hard; likely the frame used to stretch cloth for sewing robes.

carryVoice: Your line: the rains end in gifts. Something useful, never a trophy. Day one hundred fifty-five.

sources.ref: Vinaya Pitaka, Mahavagga VII.1 (Kathina Khandhaka), the thirty monks of Pava
